reason: B starts by describing the current system (the three notification types and their volumes, how MailRelay dedupes, how the broker redelivers, how flags behave), defines basic terms such as ack, terminal status and SKIP LOCKED, and lists its invariants before the steps, while A assumes the reader already knows the brief, `_deliver` and where the duplicates come from.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the current system before the plan, including what MailRelay is, how the broker and runtime flags behave, the message volumes and where duplicates come from, and it defines stack terms such as ack, lease and SKIP LOCKED; B has a good end-to-end flow and failure table but takes more for granted, leaving things like the relay, the reconciler, 'dark' and 'the brief' unexplained.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer the whole runtime picture in one compact table (parts A to F, each with its trigger, action, state and failure behaviour) and keeps it separate from the rollout steps, while A spreads the mechanics across long rollout steps, even though A defines terms like SKIP LOCKED more fully.

author: haiku
reason: A walks a newcomer through each step in plain prose (what starts it, what it does, what data it keeps, how it fails), then gives the reasons for each design choice, a sequence diagram, and one table of every limit, so I could understand the system without decoding the diagram first; B is tighter and usefully shows the table layout, but it packs most of the explanation into the diagram and a long list of notes.

author: sonnet
reason: A stands on its own: it gives full table definitions, a reason for every decision and a failure table that also says what happens to the cookie, while B uses a shortened schema and a coverage table that cites requirement numbers a newcomer never sees.

author: haiku
reason: A defines the moving parts a newcomer needs up front (key A/B, v1/v2 images, key cache, readiness) and then uses one consistent starts/does/keeps-data/on-failure structure for both the rollout and the runtime components, so the system's behaviour is easier to follow than in B, even though B helpfully puts the runtime design before the rollout.

author: haiku
reason: B gives the moving parts concrete names (key A and key B, the v1 and v2 images), lays out the startup sequence in order (the port is bound only after the keys load), and explains the mixed-fleet and rollback states, so a newcomer can follow how the system behaves at each point; A is tighter but has gaps, such as listing the CI guard as a separate rollout step after the merge that already contains it.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A explains the runtime first: how keys are loaded, used, refreshed and alerted on. It also defines terms such as workload identity before using them, so a newcomer understands the system before reading the rollout. Document B puts the rollout first, points ahead to "steps 9 to 13" for the core behavior, and relies on context the reader doesn't have, such as deploy.md and the retry-count wording.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer a better picture of the system: it explains the runtime model first (startup load, readiness, per-call reads, refresh, stale-key alert), defines workload identity, and sums up the rollout in five moves before going through it, while A puts the rollout first and explains how the app reads keys only at the end.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with a component diagram of the client, API, Postgres, queue, worker and mail provider, then gives each flow its own diagram right beside its steps, so a newcomer sees the whole system before the details; A puts all three flows into one dense diagram and never shows how the parts connect.

author: haiku
reason: A is easier to learn the system from, because it opens with a component map of every moving part and puts each flow's diagram right next to its numbered steps; B has more design depth (the worker's live-link check, the encrypted token, the login race) but puts all three diagrams in one block away from the steps and has no overview of the parts.

author: sonnet
reason: I'd rather be handed A because it puts the current system, the terms and the data model first, numbers the flow steps, and keeps "killed" links separate from "used" ones, which makes the design easier to follow than B's crowded ASCII request diagram and its reuse of used_at to kill old links.

author: sonnet
reason: I'd rather be handed B: it opens with a plain-prose overview of the existing system and the new flow, gives the data model and the "live link" rule in one place, numbers the steps in cleaner diagrams, and says honestly what is still unknown (the hash function, how emails are stored, where the breached-password list lives, whether the queue keeps payloads), while A's single tangled request diagram and its vaguer timing note are harder to follow.

author: haiku
reason: A covers the flow more completely and stays consistent from section to section: it explains each check in the main text, lists Redis and database failures in its failure table, and its account-creation step says which email goes into `users.email`. author: haiku
reason: B is the one I would rather be handed: it names every endpoint, including the confirm route, and explains why each check exists (cookie binding against login CSRF, an email match not proving ownership). author: sonnet
reason: A is easier for a newcomer to take in: it gives the schema as a commented SQL block and the state table before the flowchart, and it sends every failure to one BACK node, with a table giving each failure's message. author: haiku
reason: A explains the system more consistently and more completely: its table of where each piece of state lives and who writes it, its clear split between scheduler and attempt process, and its explicit handling of dead processes and unknown commits leave fewer gaps than B, which has a few inconsistencies such as "rollback" on failures that happen before the transaction opens and a forced-rerun skip that none of its steps performs.

author: haiku
reason: B tells a newcomer more about how the system actually works: its table shows where each piece of state lives and who writes it, it separates the scheduler from the attempt process, and it shows the merge guard in real SQL; it also covers dead processes, commits whose outcome is unknown, and manual reruns, which A either skips or lists as assumptions under "open questions".

author: sonnet
reason: A explains how the system works more completely. It defines the runner and attempts, lists every state table and its columns, and spells out how the lock works. author: sonnet
reason: B makes sense even without the diagram: it lists where each piece of state lives in a table, walks through each step with what starts it, what it does, what data it touches and what happens on failure, shows the actual merge SQL, and explains the lock and how a late commit is rejected, while A packs most of the mechanism into the flowchart and leaves things like the pipeline lock unexplained.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is easier to learn the system from: every term it uses is defined up front, the steps follow one consistent pattern, and it explains why its mechanisms are safe (for example, why sealing a day changes no rows). Document B contradicts itself (`events_clean` is called a table in one place and a view in another), states its dedup rule in a confusing way, and leaves several failure cases marked "not specified".

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to learn the system from: its idea of the winner is simple ("first copy in log order"), its day states and manifest are spelled out, and it explains why each part is safe, including each crash case, why a rewind cannot make a duplicate win, and why the seal changes no rows; A's terser dedup rule and late guard are harder for a newcomer to work through, even with its neat staging view and failure table.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: its diagram draws the live and replay paths separately, it defines "winner" as the lowest log offset and explains why, it says why the envelope keeps the IP and User-Agent, and its day close is simpler than A's seal, stale and quarantine markers, while A gives more detail on tests and owners but is harder to take in.

author: sonnet
reason: A gives a newcomer a clearer mental model: a cleaner diagram, precise terms (copy, winner by lowest offset, closed day), and the reasons behind its choices, such as keeping IP and User-Agent for replay; B is more exhaustive, but its extra seal, stale and quarantine machinery and its cramped diagram make the core flow harder to take in on a first read.
